procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A revision petition was filed before the High Court against the Trial Court's order, but no stay was granted.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court, in an order dated May 10, 2016, directed the trial court to frame charges and start the trial on a day-to-day basis. The application for cancellation of bail was repeatedly adjourned. The trial proceeded with utmost expedition pursuant to the Supreme Court's directions. The Supreme Court was approached because of a Judgment and Order dated 25.09.2012 of the High Court. The appellant-petitioner shall appear in court as and when required and shall not leave India without the previous permission of the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether it was a case where entire de novo trial is necessitated?

facts: The case involved the murder of an activist who was complaining about illegal mining.
During the trial, an unusually large number of witnesses, 105 out of 195, turned hostile.
The complainant alleged that key witnesses, including eyewitnesses, had resiled from their statements due to threats and inducement from the main accused.
The High Court, exercising its writ jurisdiction under Article 226, found that the trial had been reduced to a "farce" and ordered a complete de novo trial to prevent a failure of justice.
law: The power to order a retrial or de novo trial is an exceptional one, to be used in rare cases to avert a failure of justice.
While this power is expressly given to appellate courts under Section 386 of the Cr.P.C., the High Court can also exercise this power under its writ jurisdiction (Article 226 of the Constitution).
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's assessment that this was an exceptional case justifying a retrial.
The Court found a strong possibility that witnesses had turned hostile due to inducement or threats, which undermined the fairness of the original trial.
The Court affirmed the necessity of a new trial to ensure that witnesses could depose truthfully and fearlessly.
However, the Court considered the High Court's order for a complete re-examination of all 195 witnesses to be inappropriate and not necessary under the circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the need for a new trial but modified the High Court's order. It held that a *complete* de novo trial was not necessary. Instead, it directed a more limited retrial where only 26 crucial witnesses (8 eyewitnesses and 18 other key witnesses identified by the CBI) would be re-examined. The Court reasoned that this would be sufficient to ensure a fair trial without the burden of re-examining every witness.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court is justified in passing strictures against the Presiding Officer of the trial court?

facts: The High Court, while ordering a retrial, made adverse remarks (strictures) against the Presiding Officer of the trial court.
The High Court stated it had lost confidence in the officer and directed its administrative side to look into the matter.
The Supreme Court noted that there was no cogent evidence against the Presiding Officer to warrant such condemnation.
It was also brought to the Court's attention that the officer had rendered over 30 years of service and was on the verge of retirement.
law: A trial court judge is not supposed to be a mute spectator, especially when witnesses are turning hostile, and is expected to play an active role.
The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a High Court should not lightly pass strictures against judges in the subordinate judiciary.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's general observations about the active role a trial judge should play.
However, the Court found that condemning or "damning" the Presiding Officer was not justified in the facts of this case.
The Court reasoned that while the judge could have been more active, this error did not warrant "extreme conclusions" in the absence of any cogent evidence against him.

Considering the officer's long service and imminent retirement, and applying the principle that strictures should not be passed lightly, the Court deemed the direction for an administrative inquiry to be inappropriate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in passing the strictures. While acknowledging the judge could have been more active, the Court found the condemnation and direction for an administrative inquiry to be an extreme and inappropriate measure, especially without cogent evidence. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's direction to take up the matter against the Presiding Officer on the administrative side.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court could order retrial in exercise of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.

facts: The case before the High Court involved a criminal trial where a very large number of witnesses (105) turned hostile.
The High Court inferred that the trial had been reduced to a "farce" and a "mock trial" due to the "sheer power and position of the main accused" leading to witness tampering.
A writ application was filed under Article 226 seeking a retrial even before the trial court had pronounced its final judgment.
law: The power to order a retrial is normally exercised by an Appellate Court under Section 386 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) when reviewing the judgment of a trial court.
However, in exceptional and rare circumstances, the High Court under Article 226 (or the Supreme Court under Article 32) can also order a retrial to avert a failure of justice.

The power under Article 226 is plenary in nature, with no shackles other than self-imposed restrictions, and its extent depends on the facts of the case, with the ultimate objective of securing justice.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that this was an "exceptional case" justifying the use of writ jurisdiction.
The Court found that the "brazen highhandedness" of the accused, which led to 105 witnesses turning hostile, was a clear distortion of the judicial process.

It rejected the argument that the court should wait for the trial to conclude and for a regular appeal to be filed, stating this would "add insult to the injury" as appeals take years and the passage of time would harm the prosecution's case.

The Court held that in a situation of "monstrous perversities" and "gross abuse of process of law," the High Court cannot remain a passive onlooker and must exercise its power under Article 226 to prevent a travesty of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that while the power to order a retrial is normally vested in the Appellate Court under the Cr.P.C., the High Court was justified in exercising its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to order a retrial in this exceptional case to prevent a failure of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it was a case where entire de novo trial is necessitated?
appellant_arguments: A retrial cannot be ordered before the trial court has pronounced its judgment.
The power to order a retrial lies with the appellate court under Section 386 of the Cr.P.C., and this plea should be taken up in an appeal after the trial court's verdict.

Instead of a full retrial, the prosecuting agency had other remedies available, such as recalling witnesses under Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. or leading additional evidence in an appeal under Section 391.
The fact that witnesses turned hostile is not a sufficient reason to discard their entire evidence or order a retrial, as the trial court has yet to appreciate their testimony.
The complainant's claim that witnesses turned hostile due to threats or inducements is merely 'presumptuous and assumptious', as witnesses can turn hostile for various reasons.
The accused persons denied all allegations of threatening or inducing witnesses.
respondent_arguments: A retrial was necessary due to the tampering of prosecution witnesses through threats and inducements, which vitiated the trial process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court is justified in passing strictures against the Presiding Officer of the trial court?
appellant_arguments: The High Court should not indict the trial court proceedings or pass strictures against the judge before the trial is concluded.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's comments and strictures were justified given the circumstances of the case that warranted its intervention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court could order retrial in exercise of writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
appellant_arguments: A writ petition seeking a retrial is not maintainable.
The power to order a retrial is a statutory power of the appellate court under Section 386 of the Cr.P.C. and should not be exercised through writ jurisdiction before a judgment is delivered.
Writ proceedings are not the appropriate forum to examine disputed questions of fact, such as the allegations of witness tampering.
respondent_arguments: The High Court can exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to order a retrial to prevent a miscarriage of justice, especially when the trial process is fundamentally flawed.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The basic assumption that an accused is innocent until guilt is proven by cogent evidence is a judicial doctrine and the bedrock of criminal jurisprudence.
obiter: Performance of judicial duty in the manner prescribed by law is fundamental to the concept of rule of law in a democratic State.
The judiciary is the protector and preserver of rule of law.
A court exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution is not acting as an appellate court under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the trial was fundamentally vitiated due to an extraordinarily high number of witnesses turning hostile (105 out of 195), which was considered an eloquent, self-evident fact pointing to a miscarriage of justice. This created an exceptional circumstance justifying the High Court's intervention. The court held that in such situations, the collective interest of the community in a fair trial, where witnesses can depose truthfully and fearlessly, outweighs the individual liberty of the accused, making a retrial the only solution to prevent a travesty of justice.
legal_tests_applied: Balancing Test: The court must balance the "valuable right of liberty of an individual and the interest of the society in general." The court noted that "in a given situation, the collective interest of the community may outweigh the right of personal liberty of the individual concerned."

Exceptional Circumstances for Writ Jurisdiction: While the power to order a retrial is typically statutory, "in exceptional circumstances, such a power can be exercised by the High Court under Article 226... There are no shackles to the powers of the Constitutional Court under these provisions... these powers are plenary in nature meant to do complete justice and to inhibit travesty of justice."
why_appellant_lost: The argument that a writ petition for retrial is not maintainable was rejected because the court affirmed that the High Court's plenary powers under Article 226 can be exercised in "exceptional circumstances" to prevent a "travesty of justice," which this case was deemed to be.

The argument that hostile witnesses are an insufficient ground for retrial was rejected. The court found the fact that "as many as 105 witnesses turn hostile, out of 195 witnesses examined, is so eloquent that it does not need much effort to fathom into the reasons there for," compelling the view that a fair trial was impossible.

The argument that retrial is a premature remedy available only to an appellate court was overcome by the finding that the trial process itself was so fundamentally flawed that immediate intervention under writ jurisdiction was necessary to "protect the fair trial."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the High Court could use its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 was accepted, with the court holding that the High Court was right that this was "one of those exceptional cases where possibility of witnesses getting hostile because of inducement or threats cannot be ruled out."

The respondent's core claim that the trial was vitiated was accepted based on the sheer number of hostile witnesses, which the court found to be a cumulative fact that "compels us to take a view that in the interest of fair trial, at least crucial witnesses need to be examined again."

The High Court's decision to pass strictures against the Presiding Officer was implicitly upheld, with the Supreme Court stating its thought process was "generally in tune with the approach adopted by the High Court" and quoting the High Court's conclusion that it had "lost confidence in the present Presiding Officer."
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the need to protect the "collective interest of the community so that parties do not lose faith in the institution and indulge in private retribution."
The court stated that "There can be no more important requirement of the ends of justice than the uninterrupted progress of a fair trial."
It is necessary "to ensure that trial is conducted fairly where witnesses are able to depose truthfully and fearlessly."
The judiciary is the "protector and preserver of rule of law," and the effective functioning of this duty requires courts to conduct judicial proceedings in a way that inspires confidence.
